name: Masu-zushi (Toyama trout pressed sushi)
text: Pressed sushi of salted masu (trout) slices over vinegared rice, wrapped in bamboo (sasa) leaves and weighted. It is listed among the MAFF-selected 100 regional dishes of farming and fishing villages. Toyama City runs a Masunosushi Museum where visitors can make it by hand.
flavor: Salt-cured, firm trout against seasoned rice, with the aroma of sasa leaf.
use: Sold as a boxed ekiben and souvenir; eaten sliced from the round box, cold or at room temperature.
craft: Per the recipes found: the trout is sliced thin, sasa leaves are laid in a bent-wood (magewappa) mould, vinegared rice is spread and the fish laid on top, the leaves are folded shut, and a weight presses the box. The pressing is what bonds fish and rice. Exact salting time and rice vinegar ratios were not in the sources consulted, so confirm with a maker.

name: Toyama kaburazushi (turnip and yellowtail narezushi)
text: MAFF describes it as a narezushi-type dish: salted turnip is cut open, filled with buri (yellowtail) and similar, and slowly fermented with koji. Ingredients listed are turnip, buri, carrot and amazake koji. It is a New Year dish, and preparation starts in earnest from late November after the turnip harvest. A separate entry covers the Ishikawa (Kaga) version.
flavor: Mildly sweet, lightly sour koji ferment around crisp turnip and cured fish.
use: Served in slices as a New Year and winter dish, usually as an appetizer or side.
craft: A JA Imizuno women's section home recipe salts the turnip, then layers it with salted mackerel, carrot, ginger and chili in a rice-koji bed. It is started around mid-December so it is ready for New Year. The fish used varies by recipe (buri for MAFF, mackerel in the JA home version).
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: kaburazushi, Toyama
JA Group recipe: kaburazushi (JA Imizuno women's section)

name: Kanazawa oden
text: Oden of Kanazawa, defined by the Kanazawa Oden Shinise 50-nen-kai as using local ingredients and being served year-round. Sources disagree on origin: one gives Akadama Honten as the originator, founded 1927; Akadama's own site says its founder started serving oden in 1947. Oden Kikuichi is credited with the winter-only kani-men (crab shell stuffed with crab). Fame grew after a 2009 NHK programme named Kanazawa as having the most oden shops per capita in Japan.
flavor: Each shop has its own broth; the character comes from local ingredients.
use: Eaten at oden-ya counters year-round; kani-men is a winter item. Kuruma-fu (wheel-shaped wheat gluten) is cited by guides as a characteristic item.
craft: The age-guild definition (local ingredients, year-round) is the only formal standard found. Because shops differ in broth and ingredients, compare broth and local ingredients shop by shop. The 1927 versus 1947 dating of Akadama is unresolved in these sources.
src: Kanazawa Biyori: three features of Kanazawa oden
macaroni: Kanazawa oden shops and origin

name: Fukui sauce katsudon
text: Cutlet on rice dressed with Worcestershire-type sauce rather than egg. It is attributed to Yoroppaken, whose founder trained in Germany; the common account has him devising a sauce suited to Japanese tastes and first presenting the dish at a cooking demonstration in Tokyo in Taisho 2 (1913). Another source says it was devised in 1924 at Yoroppaken in Fukui City. Origin dates are therefore disputed.
flavor: Sweet-savoury sauce-soaked fried pork over rice, no egg binding.
use: Served as a don with the cutlet dipped in sauce; Fukui City's tourism site and local shops treat it as a signature meal.
craft: Check the sauce first: the defining feature is the house Worcestershire-style sauce. Cut thickness, crumb and frying temperature differ by shop and were not stated in the sources.

name: Heshiko (Wakasa bran-pickled fish)
text: Fish first salted and then pickled in rice bran, a preserved food of Fukui (Wakasa). The leading etymology is 'heshikomu', pressing into a barrel. It is believed to have been made since the mid-Edo period as a winter protein source, and was chosen among Japan's 100 regional dishes by MAFF in December 2007.
flavor: Strongly salty, fermented, deep umami from the bran cure.
use: Eaten as a sake snack, on ochazuke, and in modern forms found in Fukui souvenir shops.
craft: Species, salt ratio and ageing time were not given in the sources consulted.
src: Fukui City tourism: heshiko deep dive
Dear Fukui: heshiko history and making

name: Echizen oroshi soba
text: Buckwheat noodle of the Reihoku area of Fukui, where grated daikon serves as the dashi rather than as a condiment. Selected as one of MAFF's 100 regional dishes in December 2007. The leading origin theory is that a Fukui domain karo devised soba-kiri with grated daikon for poor subjects lacking soy sauce. The name is said to date from 1947, when the Showa Emperor reportedly ate two bowls.
flavor: Dark country soba with sharp, pungent grated daikon.
use: Served cold with grated daikon and tsuyu poured over; variations in daikon, dashi and toppings are common.
craft: The noodle is typically a dark inaka soba made from whole-grain (hikigurumi) flour. Judge the pungency of the daikon and its balance with the tsuyu.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: oroshi soba, Fukui

name: Hoto (Yamanashi miso noodle stew)
text: Wide flat wheat noodles simmered raw in miso broth with vegetables, chiefly kabocha; aburaage is common in homes. Chosen in 2007 as one of MAFF's 100 regional dishes. Unlike udon, no salt goes into the dough and it is not rested, and the uncooked noodles go straight into the pot. Origin theories include the sound of the old word hakutaku and Takeda Shingen cutting noodles with a family sword.
flavor: Thick, starchy, miso-sweet broth; soft vegetables dissolve into it.
use: A one-pot meal eaten hot in the cold season.
craft: The sources stress two points: no salt in the dough and no resting, with the raw noodles cooked directly in the miso broth with kabocha. Specific miso blend and noodle width were not in the sources consulted.
src: Delish Kitchen: hoto and difference from udon

name: Yoshida no udon (Fujiyoshida firm udon)
text: Udon of Fujiyoshida and the Gunnai area, noted for very hard, strongly chewy noodles and a spice paste called suridane. Standard toppings are cabbage and horse meat in a broth combining miso and soy. Horse-meat food culture around Fujiyoshida is linked to the horse's role in Mt. Fuji climbing and farming. It is also on MAFF's list of 100 regional dishes.
flavor: Extremely firm, chewy noodle with a hot, spiced miso-soy broth.
use: Served hot or cold; the suridane is added at the table.
craft: Texture is the criterion: noodles are judged by firmness and chew. Exact flour, water and kneading figures were not in the sources.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Yoshida no udon

name: Kofu torimotsu-ni (glazed chicken offal)
text: Chicken offal (liver, gizzard, heart, kinkan unlaid eggs, himo) simmered fast over high heat in a small amount of sweet-savoury tare until glazed. The method is noted as unlike ordinary motsu-ni. It won the B-1 Grand Prix and is listed in MAFF's regional dishes database.
flavor: Glossy, sweet-salty glaze that concentrates the sweetness and umami of the offal.
use: Served as a side dish or sake snack in soba shops and izakaya.
craft: The key point in the sources is short cooking time at high heat with little liquid, to reduce the sauce and keep the offal tender. Sauce ratios were not given.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: torimotsu-ni, Yamanashi
Kyodo ryori 100: hoto and Yamanashi dishes

name: Oyaki (Nagano stuffed dumpling)
text: Dough of wheat or buckwheat flour wrapped around vegetables or sweet bean paste and baked. In mountain areas wheat and buckwheat were widely grown, and flour dishes stood in for rice. MAFF notes traces of baked millet-flour dough at a Jomon site in Ogawa village as a possible origin. In the Hokushin area it has been made as an Obon offering. Newer forms, including French-style, are reported.
flavor: Chewy, floury skin with savoury vegetable or sweet filling.
use: Eaten as a snack or light meal, warm; sold at roadside and tourist shops.
craft: Dough type (wheat, buckwheat or mixed) and cooking (baked, steamed, or both) vary by district; these specifics were not detailed in the sources consulted.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: oyaki, Nagano

name: Gohei-mochi (Kiso and Ina skewered rice cake)
text: Half-pounded non-glutinous (uruchi) rice shaped onto skewers, brushed with miso or soy tare and grilled. Centred on the Kiso and Ina areas per MAFF. Name theories: resemblance to the gohei ritual paper offering, or a man named Gohei. It is said to have existed by the mid-Edo period. In Anan town the gohei-shaped cake is recorded as an offering to the gods from the Edo period.
flavor: Chewy grain texture of partly pounded rice with a toasty miso or soy glaze.
use: Eaten as a snack or festival food, grilled to order.
craft: Half-pounded (hangoroshi) rice keeps grain texture, so judge the pounding stage. Shapes and tare differ by region and were not detailed in the sources.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: gohei-mochi, Nagano
Agency for Cultural Affairs: Nagano 100-year food list

name: Basashi (Nagano raw horse meat)
text: Thin slices of fresh lean horse meat eaten raw with garlic soy sauce or ginger soy sauce. One source describes Nagano as a heavy consumer of horse meat and basashi as an izakaya staple deeply rooted among residents.
flavor: Lean, clean red meat; garlic or ginger sharpens it.
use: Served as a cold plate in izakaya with garlic or ginger soy.
craft: Freshness is the premise given in the source; cut thickness and grade distinctions were not stated.
src: Suzaka News: Nagano local gourmet guide

name: Inago and hachinoko tsukudani (Ina valley insect foods)
ja: イナゴ・蜂の子の佃煮
text: In the Ina valley and elsewhere in Nagano, grasshoppers (inago) and bee larvae (hachinoko) were eaten, especially in wartime and food shortages. Inago tsukudani remains a familiar food around the rice-harvest season.
flavor: Sweet-salty soy simmer; the sources give no sensory detail.
use: Eaten as a side dish or with rice, as preserved tsukudani.
craft: Specific cooking ratios were not found. Treat as a seasonal foraged preserve.
src: Hatagomaruhachi: guide to Nagano local dishes

name: Hoba-miso (Hida magnolia-leaf miso)
text: Homemade koji miso grilled on a dried magnolia (hoba) leaf, a dish of Hida and Takayama. By one account it began with forestry workers using the leaf as a plate to grill miso; it spread to households and was sold as a souvenir from the 1960s (Showa 40s). Negi and shiitake are grilled with the miso.
flavor: Smoky, aromatic miso with leaf fragrance; sweet-savoury.
use: Eaten over rice, grilled at table on a small brazier or hot plate.
craft: Charcoal is said to be best; a hot plate or frying pan works as a substitute. The leaf holds the miso from burning directly on the heat.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: hoba-miso, Gifu

name: Keichan / Tori-chan (Gifu miso-marinated chicken)
text: Chicken stir-fried with cabbage, carrot and green pepper after marinating in a miso-based tare. Sources date its birth to about 1950 and say local butchers and izakaya added their own seasonings from about 1960. Theories: a copy of jingisukan eaten in parts of Gifu, or a way to eat laying hens past their prime in and after the war. Names and tare differ by area.
flavor: Garlicky, miso-savoury chicken with sweet cooked vegetables.
use: Cooked on a griddle or pan at home or izakaya, eaten with rice.
craft: An example recipe marinates the chicken in miso, sake, light soy and grated garlic. Salt, soy or miso bases vary by region.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: tori-chan, Gifu

name: Shizuoka oden
text: Skewered oden simmered in a dark broth and finished with aonori and fish powder (dashiko). MAFF dates its start to the Taisho period; after WWII discarded beef tendon and pork offal became ingredients. Suruga Bay fish let fish-paste items such as black hanpen be used. Black hanpen is made from mackerel and sardine with skin and bones, hence the grey colour, and is associated with Yaizu.
flavor: Dark soy and beef-tendon broth, savoury and rich.
use: Sold at dagashi shops and oden stands, eaten off the skewer.
craft: The Shizuoka Oden Association's five rules: black hanpen, black broth, skewers, aonori and dashiko, sold at dagashi shops. The broth is based on dark soy sauce and beef-tendon stock and topped up daily.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Shizuoka oden
Umibose: five rules of Shizuoka oden

name: Miso-nikomi udon (Nagoya)
text: Udon simmered in a pot with miso broth, a Nagoya-meshi staple. Ota-ya Honten of Ichinomiya is cited as the originator. Theories on origin: derived from Yamanashi hoto, brought to Mikawa by Takeda retainers in the Sengoku period, or made by textile mill women in Ichinomiya in the Meiji era.
flavor: Strong, dark miso broth.
use: Served bubbling in a lidded earthenware pot.
craft: Broth and noodle specifications were not found in the sources consulted. Origin remains disputed.

name: Kishimen (Nagoya flat noodle)
text: Flat wheat noodle associated with Nagoya. Imogawa Udon of Kariya is cited as the origin. Name theories: kijimen (pheasant meat), Kishu noodle, a theory based on the characters 棊子麺. The Nagoya board of education considers kijimen the most likely. Only the Nagoya area uses the name 'kishimen'.
flavor: Smooth, flat noodle; sources give no further detail.
use: Served hot in broth or cold, with toppings.
craft: Width and flour specifications were not in the sources.

name: Ankake spaghetti (Nagoya)
ja: あんかけスパゲッティ
text: Spaghetti with a thick, spiced sauce, a Nagoya B-grade dish. Yokoi (Spaghetti House Yokoi), founded in 1963, is considered the originator. The name is attributed to Karameya's first owner, inspired by ankake udon.
flavor: Thick, peppery sauce over noodles.
use: Served on a hot plate with toppings.
craft: Sauce composition was not found in the sources.

name: Nagoya tebasaki (fried chicken wings)
text: Fried chicken wings, classed as Nagoya-meshi originating in Nagoya City. Which shop invented it is disputed in the sources.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Izakaya dish, eaten by hand.
craft: Sauce and frying specs were not found. Origin shop is unresolved.

name: Ogura toast (Nagoya kissaten)
text: Toast spread with sweet azuki paste (ogura-an), said to have been born in a Nagoya kissaten in the Taisho period (1920s). Sources note differing claims on the original shop and date.
flavor: Sweet red bean over toasted bread.
use: Served at kissaten, often with morning sets.
craft: Butter and bread type were not covered by the sources.

name: Nagoya-meshi (the category)
text: The label for foods originating in or developed in the Nagoya (Chukyo) area, including miso-katsu, hitsumabushi, tebasaki, kishimen, miso-nikomi udon and ankake spaghetti. The term settled around 2001, credited to Inamoto Kenichi of Zetton. It is a marketing category, not a single cuisine.
flavor: Often strong in miso, sweetness and sauce; the label is a category.
use: Used for tourism and restaurant branding.
craft: Individual dishes have separate origin disputes, so check each dish by itself.

name: Tekone-zushi (Mie hand-mixed sushi)
text: Sushi of lean fish such as katsuo or maguro, with vinegared rice, listed in MAFF's 100 regional dishes. Fishermen cut fish on the boat and mixed it by hand, hence the name. Mie has a large katsuo catch. Another account links it to Ise-Shima ama divers. One source says that until about Showa 20 only fish slices were laid on top, and nori and other toppings were added from the 1950s.
flavor: Lean red fish over vinegared rice.
use: Eaten as a one-bowl meal.
craft: Fish is mixed with the rice by hand. Marinade ratios were not found.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: tekone-zushi, Mie

name: Ise udon
text: Thick, soft udon with a little tamari-based sauce. Origin is unclear; before the Edo period the Ise area ate thick, chewless udon with tamari from jimiso. During Edo-period Ise pilgrimage it became a simple dish served quickly. The name was fixed in 1972 by the Ise noodle trade association. Registration criteria cited by Wikipedia: total thickness 6 mm or more, boiled 25 minutes or more.
flavor: Soft noodle, dark sauce that tastes less salty than it looks, with strong umami and sweetness.
use: Served with the sauce and chopped negi on top.
craft: Tamari sauce is typically tamari with katsuo dashi. Judge noodle softness and sauce balance, not firmness.
